choices: Justice should focus on pain because prevention sounds too soft to protect anyone.
Justice should avoid prevention because causal understanding weakens public safety.
Justice should focus on prevention because causal understanding points toward reducing future harm.
questions.explanation: The humane model treats prevention as serious justice. It follows causes to lower future harm rather than equating justice with cruelty.

reviewCards.front: What does biological mitigation without fatalism ask a justice system to do?
reviewCards.back: It asks the system to weigh changed capacity without treating harm as harmless. The response should protect people, repair where possible, and prevent future harm.

reviewCards.front: Why does the Charles Whitman tumor case complicate blame without settling it?
reviewCards.back: After the 1966 University of Texas shooting, the autopsy found a tumor near regions tied to emotion regulation. That can matter causally without erasing victims or context.

reviewCards.front: How can frontal-lobe damage change the legal question?
reviewCards.back: Frontal damage can weaken inhibition and social judgment. The legal question shifts from character alone to what control remained and what restraint or support fits.

reviewCards.front: What part of punishment does Anthony Cashmore's free-will argument challenge most directly?
reviewCards.back: Anthony Cashmore's 2010 PNAS argument challenges desert-based revenge, the idea that pain is owed because a person could have chosen outside biology. It leaves public safety and prevention available.

reviewCards.front: Why must risk assessment stay cautious even when biology helps prediction?
reviewCards.back: Risk is probabilistic, not certain. A prediction error can restrict someone for a future act that would not happen, so prevention needs review and guardrails.

reviewCards.front: Recall embodied metaphor and moral judgment (Ch 15): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Maelle hears "Justice must hurt to count." The pain metaphor steers the room toward vengeance, while the safer question asks whether prevention can count as serious justice.

implementationPlan.title: Run the Blame-to-Prevention Tally
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching the jump from harm to pure blame. Run the Blame-to-Prevention Tally by marking the blame thought, naming the capacity question, and choosing the safety response. The skill is firm without being cruel.

ifThenPlans.context: If you hear yourself call a loss of control pure character.
ifThenPlans.plan: If control is the issue, then run the Blame-to-Prevention Tally. Ask what brake may be damaged and what boundary still protects people.

ifThenPlans.context: If free-will doubt makes you fear that accountability is gone.
ifThenPlans.plan: If accountability feels at risk, then run the Blame-to-Prevention Tally. Mark the blame thought, ask what capacity is in question, then choose the safety response.

ifThenPlans.context: If a cause makes a person's conduct seem fixed forever.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you spot a cause, then ask what could change it. Look for one environment, treatment, or supervision change that lowers future harm.

ifThenPlans.context: If an explanation sounds like an insult to the harmed person.
ifThenPlans.plan: If explanation feels disloyal, then state the harm first. Then ask what capacity fact changes the response without denying the injury.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next day, count every time you move from "they chose it" to pure blame. Tally the count, then circle each case where a capacity question would change the response.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Across this week, tally each moment you equate seriousness with suffering. At week's end, read the number and choose one case where prevention would have been firmer.

chapters.title: War and Peace
chapters.hook: 1914: the dugout table still held cold tins after enemies had climbed out to meet.
chapters.counterintuition: You may expect war to mean hatred has filled every corner. In fact, the same group instincts can harden a border or widen it when the setting changes.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next conversation about a shared risk, use the first 10 minutes to put a check mark in the margin when someone names fear before blame.
chapters.keyTakeaway: War grows when groups make harm feel permitted; peace lasts when institutions, memory, and shared futures make restraint safer than revenge.

breakdown.fastRead:
Gemma stands in a Western Front dugout in 1914, after the singing has crossed the mud and before anyone knows what to call it. The easy story says enemies stay enemies because hate fills them from boot to helmet. In fact, shared ritual can loosen that label for a while. A border in the mind can move.

War is still brutal. It means biology is conditional. The same brain that can obey, fear, and dehumanize can also notice a voice, copy a norm, and imagine tomorrow. Peace is built before the beautiful moment. If you wait until the rifle is raised, you are already late.
breakdown.deepRead:
Sophie has the South Africa hearing list in front of her, and every name on it carries somebody's dead. This is where the mechanism gets harder than a holiday truce. Contact alone is not enough. People need a public way to say what happened, a rule for what follows, and a future that does not make the next attack feel sensible.

A uniformed crowd can use the same social tools for opposite ends. Coalition, or group loyalty, can shrink the circle until only your side counts. Obedience can make a uniform feel like permission. Fear can turn a rumor into a reason to strike first. But those same tools can be steered. Loyalty can protect a cease-fire. Rules can make restraint less lonely. Public memory can stop the past from leaking poison into every new meeting.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission in South Africa carried that mixed load. It did not pretend that pain vanished when people sat in a room. It used testimony and conditional amnesty to put memory in public while trying to avoid a wider civil war. Memory can heal only when it stays honest.

In 1998 Northern Ireland, the agreement adds another piece. A handshake is fragile if each side thinks the other can break it and win. Shared offices and consent rules gave rival groups something to lose if the deal burned. That is why peace is not just a mood. It is a set of conditions that makes the calmer act less reckless than the violent one.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jeanne reads the phrase "they will never change" and knows how neat it sounds. It is the kind of sentence that feels tough because it skips all the work. If humans are simply warlike, you do not have to ask who is selling threat, who gains from humiliation, or which rules make betrayal pay.

A checkpoint guard can sort people into us and them before he has finished a sentence. Humans copy strong signals from their own side. We can obey leaders, defend honor, and narrow care until a stranger becomes a target. Dehumanization matters because it changes who seems protected. Once a person is described as less than fully human, harm needs less permission.

A trench on the Western Front will not let you stop with the harsh story. Parts of the line paused in 1914. Soldiers who had been ordered to kill sometimes exchanged greetings and stepped into no-man's-land. The truce did not end World War I. It did show that enemy identity is not always total. Direct contact and shared ritual can interrupt the official story long enough for a person to see a person.

A South Africa hearing room shows a slower version. Public testimony did not undo apartheid violence. Conditional amnesty did not satisfy every demand for punishment. Still, the process gave memory a shape that was neither blanket revenge nor forced forgetting. That matters because unaddressed atrocity does not stay quiet. It waits inside families, elections, police stops, and rumors.

A Northern Ireland draft shows the institutional side. The Good Friday Agreement did not rely on everyone waking up kinder in 1998. It built power sharing and consent into the political future. That changed the cost of walking away. When rival groups have a stake in the system, restraint can feel less like surrender and more like self-protection.

You draft a message about a family argument, then see the old pattern: prove your side first, repair later if there is time. The modern cost is not a battlefield. It is the sister you meant to check on, the appointment you forgot, and the day gone with ten half-finished fights in your head. You write one word in the phone margin before calling: future. The word does not make you noble. It reminds you to ask what would make tomorrow safer for both sides.

A soldier waving a white cloth can still be bait. If armed men use a truce signal to lure soldiers forward, obeying the pull of contact would be a mistake. If a hearing room lets known killers threaten witnesses, memory has become a trap. Stop the harm first. Restraint needs conditions, and danger sometimes means the first condition is distance.

examples.title: Mud Before Song
examples.scenario: Cold mud presses through soldier Gemma's boot sole in the Western Front dugout, and the song outside costs her the whole hour. It is 1914, World War I, and the next minutes can go to scanning rifles, answering the carol, or warning the trench. No one has climbed out yet. Gemma decides alone where attention goes before the truce has any shape.
examples.whatToDo: Gemma keeps one ear on the line and one ear on the singing. She writes the next watch order so contact can be tested without leaving the trench blind.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning comes before courage. The scene shows that human contact can soften an enemy label only when attention still protects real danger.

examples.title: Hearing List Choice
examples.scenario: Clerk Sophie lowers the hearing folder before the first witness walks into the South Africa room. One path gives every demand for punishment full weight and risks turning the transition into revenge. The other path asks families to forget too much. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission offers a narrow third line: public testimony with conditional amnesty. Sophie has to choose how the session will hold both pain and restraint.
examples.whatToDo: Sophie marks testimony first, amnesty only under conditions, and no silence about the harm. She refuses to let revenge or forgetting own the room.
examples.whyItMatters: The dilemma makes the lesson practical. Peace often needs a hybrid form that remembers injury while lowering the odds of renewed violence.

examples.title: Draft Across the Table
examples.scenario: Jeanne slides the draft back in 1998 Northern Ireland while Landon is still reading the power sharing clause. "If they get seats, they can block us," she says. Landon taps the consent line. "If they get none, they can leave the table." "So we are rewarding threat?" "No. We are making the future too useful to burn." The Good Friday Agreement is still paper, but the old victory script has lost its clean ending.
examples.whatToDo: Jeanne keeps the power sharing clause in the draft and asks Landon to tighten the consent language. They make restraint part of the deal's structure.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows why peace needs more than goodwill. Institutions matter when fear of betrayal would make violence look rational.

examples.title: Carol Instead of Trap
examples.scenario: Guard Amelie is three words into the warning when another voice rises from the enemy trench. She expects a trick. In World War I, that expectation keeps people alive. Then the sound gathers into a carol, and the reply from her own side changes the air before any order can explain it. The Christmas Truce of 1914 begins as a broken prediction: the enemy signal is not only a threat.
examples.whatToDo: Amelie keeps the warning ready but stops calling the song proof of attack. She lets the new evidence change the category before the next order arrives.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal teaches a narrow skill. You do not drop caution, but you update when contact gives you evidence that the threat story is incomplete.

examples.title: 1998 Thread
examples.scenario:
1998. Clerk Adam's returned call becomes a text thread when the Northern Ireland line keeps dropping.
Draft desk: Consent line stays?
Adam: It has to.
Draft desk: They will say it slows change.
Adam: It also lowers fear.
Draft desk: Power sharing too?
Adam: Yes. If the future has seats, walking away costs more.
Draft desk: Then keep both.
examples.whatToDo: Adam argues for consent and power sharing in the shortest possible terms. He keeps the draft tied to future stakes, not to a promise of nicer feelings.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread lands the mechanism between the lines. Peace lasts longer when each side can see a safer future inside the same system.

examples.title: Testimony Reset
examples.scenario: Every 1995 hearing schedule had begun to look tidy, and that was the problem. Coordinator Sierra reads the next South Africa testimony block and hears the Truth and Reconciliation Commission routine flatten. Name, harm, question, amnesty note. She stops the clerk before the witness is called. "Start again," she says. "First the harm in public words, then the condition for amnesty. Nobody gets to call this forgetting."
examples.whatToDo: Sierra interrupts the routine and rewrites the order aloud. She puts acknowledgment before process so conditional amnesty does not erase the injury.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset shows why accountability belongs inside peace work. A process that hides harm can preserve the very revenge cycle it hopes to end.

questions.prompt: A leader describes the other side as less than fully human before a raid. Which risk best fits the danger Sapolsky is tracking?
choices: The label can narrow who seems protected, making mass harm easier to permit.
The label mainly proves that every soldier already hated the enemy in private.
The label matters only after violence begins, when people search for excuses.
questions.explanation: The fact centers dehumanization before the final act. It lowers the moral threshold by changing who counts as protected, not by proving innate hatred.

questions.prompt: "Enemy identity is total once a war starts." Which reading best fits the Christmas Truce evidence?
choices: It shows war stops once enough soldiers discover they have the same rituals.
It shows shared contact can interrupt enemy categories under some conditions.
It shows official categories matter less than personal courage in every battle.
questions.explanation: The truce was temporary and conditional. Direct contact and shared ritual softened categories, but they did not end the war or make danger disappear.

questions.prompt: A peace draft says, "Once both sides want calm, institutions can wait." Which response best names the likely failure?
choices: The draft may overvalue public testimony and understate private grief.
The draft may leave betrayal fears strong enough to make violence seem rational.
The draft may create too many shared stakes and make conflict harder to name.
questions.explanation: The supported answer is about credible institutions. A change of heart is fragile if each side still fears that restraint leaves it exposed.

questions.prompt: After apartheid, a planner says society must choose trials for everyone or silence about the past. Which reply fits the South Africa case?
choices: Public testimony with conditional amnesty can hold memory and restraint together.
Public testimony should wait until every demand for punishment has been settled.
Conditional amnesty works best when testimony avoids naming specific harms.
questions.explanation: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission is the hybrid case. It used acknowledgment and conditional amnesty rather than pure revenge or forgetting.

questions.prompt: A winning side wants to impose peace and keep rivals outside the new system. Which outcome does the source fact warn about?
choices: Rivals may accept exclusion if the winner promises faster order.
Rivals may forget past losses once violence becomes too costly.
Rivals may return to violence when the future offers them no stake.
questions.explanation: Power sharing gives groups a reason to protect the future system. Exclusion can leave incentives hostile, so imposed peace may not hold.

questions.prompt: "Humans are uniformly warlike, so prevention is cosmetic." Which response best challenges that line?
choices: Violence varies with governance, norms, resources, and institutions.
Violence appears whenever biology is discussed in public terms.
Violence falls only when leaders replace old memories with new slogans.
questions.explanation: The fact points to variation across societies and eras. If rates and forms change with context, prevention can work upstream of the crisis.

questions.prompt: A group says loyalty can only fuel violence. Which move best tests the claim in a cease-fire plan?
choices: Ask members to drop all group identity before any agreement begins.
Frame restraint as private kindness with no link to group honor.
Redirect loyalty toward protecting a shared cease-fire and future.
questions.explanation: Coalitional psychology can serve peace when shared identity widens or shifts. The answer keeps loyalty but points it toward restraint.

questions.prompt: A negotiator says, "Peace requires ignoring the past so everyone can move on." What should the group infer first?
choices: It misses that punishment must come before any public memory can matter.
It misses that contact alone dissolves old grievance once groups meet.
It misses that unaddressed atrocity can keep revenge cycles alive.
questions.explanation: Accountability matters because buried atrocity can preserve grievance. Memory can support repair when it is organized in public, not ignored.

questions.prompt: A reader says biological roots make peace impossible. Which response best reflects Sapolsky's biology?
choices: Biology mainly explains aggression, while peace begins when biology is suppressed.
Biology supports aggression, empathy, norm following, and future planning.
Biology makes optimism safe only when institutions reduce fear first.
questions.explanation: The source fact is conditional. The same human capacities can support harm or peace, depending on incentives, norms, identity, and future expectations.

reviewCards.front: What does conditional violence and reconciliation mean in plain language?
reviewCards.back: The same human tools can feed war or peace. Fear, obedience, loyalty, empathy, rules, and future planning change their effect when the setting changes.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more for war and peace, evolved behavioral strategies (Ch 10) or conditional reconciliation, and why?
reviewCards.back: Ch 10 explains why flexible social capacities exist. War and peace ask which setting steers those capacities toward harm or restraint, so the harder call depends more on conditions.

reviewCards.front: Why does the Christmas Truce not prove that war is fake?
reviewCards.back: On the Western Front in 1914, the truce was temporary and partial. It shows enemy labels can soften through shared ritual while World War I still remains.

reviewCards.front: Why did the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission matter for peace?
reviewCards.back: It joined public testimony with conditional amnesty. That mix kept memory visible while trying to reduce the chance that punishment demands would restart wider violence.

reviewCards.front: What did the Good Friday Agreement add that a handshake could not?
reviewCards.back: In 1998 Northern Ireland, it built power sharing and consent into the future. Those structures made restraint safer because rivals had a stake in the same system.

reviewCards.front: When does contact across a group line become too naive?
reviewCards.back: Contact is unsafe when one side can use it to trap, threaten, or erase the other. Restraint needs conditions, and sometimes distance is the first condition.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the Safer Future
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice asking what would make restraint feel safe before you ask who deserves blame. Use one visible mark to pull your attention toward future stakes, public memory, and fair rules. The mark is small on purpose; it gives your next sentence a job.

ifThenPlans.context: If a conversation starts sorting people into good side and bad side,
ifThenPlans.plan: then ask what rule would protect both sides from betrayal. Keep the question concrete enough that someone could answer it.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone says the past should be ignored,
ifThenPlans.plan: then ask what harm still needs public words. Do not let repair become forced forgetting.

ifThenPlans.context: If anger makes punishment feel like the whole answer,
ifThenPlans.plan: then ask what future would still be safe after punishment. Hold accountability and restraint in the same sentence.

ifThenPlans.context: If a shared plan depends only on goodwill,
ifThenPlans.plan: then name the institution, rule, or check that would make betrayal less useful. Peace needs a structure, not just a mood.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During your next conversation about a shared risk, write FUTURE on a margin or sticky note. Add one tick when you ask what would make restraint safe.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, swap one habit: before proving your side first, ask what rule or future stake would lower fear. Compare the old habit and the swap at week's end.
